p: Both galleries live in grand old buildings that weren't built for art. Modern One is housed in a former school, while Modern Two started life as an orphanage, and the classical architecture makes a striking backdrop for the bold work inside. In front of Modern One, the lawn has been sculpted by the landscape architect Charles Jencks into a landform of curving grassy terraces and crescent-shaped pools. Kids love running along the ridges, and it's a cracking spot for photos.

Modern Two is home to a much-loved recreation of the studio of Eduardo Paolozzi, the Edinburgh-born sculptor, packed with plaster casts, tools and half-finished pieces. You'll also find his giant Vulcan figure looming over the space. The collection is strong on Surrealism too, so expect a few surprises from artists such as Dalí and Magritte.

Entry to the collection is free, with some exhibitions charged. Allow two to three hours to see both buildings properly, and keep the café in mind for a halfway breather. Buses from the city centre stop nearby on Belford Road, or it's a walk of around twenty to thirty minutes from Princes Street, partly downhill on the way there and uphill coming back.

If you do follow the Water of Leith down to Dean Village, the old mill buildings and riverside cottages make one of the prettiest corners of the city. From there, Stockbridge, with its independent shops and Sunday market, is a short walk on, making for a gorgeous half day away from the busiest streets.
